question: What does a fractional CRO actually do?
body:
## Direct Answer
A fractional CRO is a part-time Chief Revenue Officer who owns a company's entire revenue engine — sales, marketing alignment, RevOps, and customer success — for a fraction of a full-time executive's cost and hours. They typically work one to three days a week per client, install repeatable revenue systems, coach the existing team, and hand the machine back once it runs on its own. The role is outcome-first: pipeline built, forecast accuracy raised, and go-to-market motion fixed, not seat-warming.

Most founders hire a fractional CRO when revenue has stalled somewhere between one and twenty million in ARR and the gap is no longer "we need more leads" but "we have no system that reliably turns leads into closed, retained revenue." A good fractional CRO diagnoses that system in weeks, rebuilds the broken segments of it, and installs the operating cadence that keeps it healthy after they leave. The rest of this essay breaks down exactly what those weeks look like, what the work actually produces, and how to tell a real revenue leader from an expensive coach.

## What is a fractional CRO and how is it different from a consultant or a VP of Sales
A fractional CRO carries the accountability of a full-time revenue chief while working part-time across one or a few companies. The distinction that matters is ownership. A consultant delivers a recommendation deck and leaves; a VP of Sales owns one function — the sellers — and reports up. A fractional CRO owns the whole revenue number and every function that feeds it: demand generation, pipeline, sales execution, revenue operations, pricing, and net retention. They sit at the executive table, present to the board, and are measured on the same metrics a full-time CRO would be.

The "fractional" part is about time and cost, not seniority. These are usually operators with fifteen-plus years of experience who have already been a full-time CRO or VP of Revenue at least once, and who now split their attention deliberately. For a company doing three million in ARR, a full-time CRO at three hundred thousand-plus in base plus equity is both unaffordable and overkill — there isn't enough complexity yet to justify a full week of executive time. A fractional engagement gives that company senior judgment for the ten or fifteen hours a week where it actually moves the number. This is the same logic that drives the broader shift toward fractional revenue leadership documented at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-vs-full-time.

The difference from a "fractional VP of Sales" is scope. A fractional sales leader will fix your close rate and your rep ramp. A fractional CRO will do that too, but will also ask why marketing is passing leads that never convert, why customer success is losing ten percent of ARR to churn, and why the forecast is wrong every quarter. The CRO title signals that the person is empowered to fix the seams between functions, which is usually where mid-stage revenue actually leaks.

It also helps to name what a fractional CRO is *not*, because the market is crowded with adjacent titles that sound similar and cost differently. They are not a lead-generation agency that promises to fill the top of the funnel; those firms are paid for volume and have no stake in whether that volume ever becomes revenue. They are not a sales-training vendor who runs a two-day workshop and disappears; training without a system to reinforce it evaporates within a quarter. And they are not an interim executive hired to keep a seat warm while the company runs a full-time search — an interim leader is measured on continuity, whereas a fractional CRO is measured on transformation. The mental model that works best is "a senior operator on a time-boxed mission," where the mission is a specific, agreed-upon change to how revenue is produced, and the time-box is the discipline that keeps the engagement honest.

One more distinction worth drawing is between a fractional CRO and a board advisor or investor who "helps with go-to-market." Advisors are valuable, but they operate at the level of opinion and introductions; they do not open the CRM, restage the pipeline, or sit on a Tuesday-morning forecast call and challenge a rep's commit. The defining feature of the fractional CRO is that they do the work inside the company's own systems, with the company's own people, on the company's own deals. That hands-in-the-machine quality is exactly what makes the role expensive relative to advice, and exactly what makes it worth the money when the underlying problem is operational rather than strategic.

## What does a fractional CRO do in the first 90 days
The first ninety days are diagnostic-then-surgical. A competent fractional CRO does not walk in and start selling. They walk in and build a map of how revenue currently flows — or fails to — and then they cut into the two or three segments that are bleeding the most. The sequence below is the standard shape of a well-run engagement, though the specific fixes vary wildly by company.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Days 1 to 30 Diagnose] --> B[Audit pipeline and CRM data]
    A --> C[Interview reps and customers]
    A --> D[Rebuild forecast from raw deals]
    B --> E[Days 31 to 60 Design]
    C --> E
    D --> E
    E --> F[Fix ICP and sales stages]
    E --> G[Rewrite comp and territory plan]
    F --> H[Days 61 to 90 Install]
    G --> H
    H --> I[Run weekly forecast cadence]
    H --> J[Coach reps live on deals]
    I --> K[Handoff to durable system]
    J --> K
```

In the first thirty days the work is almost entirely listening and counting. The CRO pulls the CRM apart to see whether the pipeline is real, sits in on live sales calls, and interviews both the reps and a sample of won and lost customers. The single most common finding at this stage is that the reported pipeline is fiction — deals sit in stages that mean nothing, close dates slip indefinitely, and the "forecast" is a hope-weighted guess. Rebuilding the forecast bottom-up from actual deal evidence is often the first hard artifact a fractional CRO delivers, and it is frequently the moment a founder realizes the revenue problem is a systems problem, not an effort problem. The mechanics of that rebuild are covered at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/forecast-accuracy-rebuild.

The diagnostic phase is deliberately unglamorous, and a founder who expects instant activity can misread it as slowness. What is actually happening is evidence-gathering under a specific discipline: every claim the company makes about its own revenue gets checked against the underlying data. Does the reported win rate hold up when you exclude deals that were never really qualified? Is the average sales cycle the number leadership quotes, or is that number distorted by a handful of fast, referral-driven closes that mask a much longer motion for cold accounts? How much of last quarter's number came from one or two heroic reps whose behavior can't be systematized? A good fractional CRO leaves the first month with a small number of load-bearing truths — usually uncomfortable ones — that reframe the entire conversation about where revenue is actually breaking.

Days thirty-one to sixty are design. Having seen where deals die, the CRO redefines the ideal customer profile so reps stop chasing accounts that never close, rewrites the sales stages so each one has an exit criterion tied to buyer behavior, and usually touches the comp plan and territory model — because you cannot change what reps do without changing what they are paid to do. This is delicate work; a botched comp change can trigger rep attrition faster than any other single move, which is why an experienced operator sequences it carefully rather than rewriting everything at once.

The design phase is also where the fractional CRO decides what *not* to fix, and that restraint is a skill in itself. A first-time internal leader tends to attack every visible flaw at once, which overwhelms the team and produces change fatigue without measurable improvement. A seasoned operator ranks the fixes by leverage — which single change moves the number most, with the least disruption — and sequences the rest behind it. Often the highest-leverage fix is not a new tactic at all but the removal of something: a bloated pipeline stage that hides stalled deals, a compensation kicker that rewards discounting, a "qualified lead" definition so loose that it guarantees wasted rep hours. Subtraction, done deliberately, frequently outperforms addition in the first quarter.

Days sixty-one to ninety are installation and coaching. The new system only sticks if the CRO runs it live: a weekly forecast call with real deal inspection, live coaching on active opportunities, and a scoreboard the whole team can see. By the end of the first quarter the company should have a forecast it can trust within a reasonable band, a pipeline that reflects reality, and a repeatable motion the internal team can run without the CRO in the room every day.

Installation is where most engagements are won or lost, because a system that exists only in a slide deck is worthless. The forecast call is the keystone ritual: run consistently, with real deal inspection and honest commit-versus-best-case discipline, it retrains the entire team's instincts about what a real deal looks like within about six to eight weeks. The CRO's job during this phase is to model the behavior they want to become permanent — asking the hard qualification questions out loud, praising accurate pessimism over optimistic slippage, and making the scoreboard visible enough that the team self-corrects without being told. The goal is not the CRO's presence but the CRO's absence: a cadence robust enough to survive their departure.

## What functions does a fractional CRO actually own
The reason the title is "revenue officer" and not "sales officer" is that a fractional CRO is responsible for the entire arc from a stranger's first impression to an expanded, renewed customer. Owning that whole arc is what separates the role from any single functional leader, and it is where the highest-leverage fixes usually live — in the handoffs between teams that no single VP is incentivized to own.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Marketing demand] --> B[Sales pipeline]
    B --> C[Sales execution and close]
    C --> D[Customer success and retention]
    D --> E[Expansion and renewal]
    E --> A
    F[RevOps and data spine] --> A
    F --> B
    F --> C
    F --> D
```

On the demand side, the fractional CRO does not usually run campaigns, but they enforce the definition of a qualified lead and hold marketing accountable for pipeline contribution rather than raw lead volume. On the sales side they own methodology, stage discipline, deal coaching, and the comp plan. Underneath all of it sits revenue operations — the data spine that makes the CRM trustworthy, the reporting honest, and the forecast repeatable. Many fractional CRO engagements are, in practice, RevOps rescue missions wearing an executive title, because the underlying data was too broken to run a company on. The connective role RevOps plays across every function is detailed at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-as-connective-tissue.

The handoffs deserve special emphasis because they are the part of the revenue engine that literally no one owns by default. Marketing is measured on leads, sales on closed deals, and customer success on retention — and each function optimizes its own metric right up to the boundary where it passes work to the next team, then stops caring. The result is predictable: marketing celebrates a record lead month while sales quietly ignores most of those leads as junk; sales closes an aggressive deal with promises the product can't keep, and customer success inherits a churn risk it had no say in creating. A fractional CRO's most distinctive contribution is standing across all of those boundaries at once and being the single person paid to make the handoffs clean. That is why the role so often produces gains that surprise the founder — the leaks were never inside a function, they were between functions, invisible to everyone whose incentive stopped at the wall.

On the retention side, a strong fractional CRO refuses to treat customer success as someone else's problem. If a company is acquiring customers at a healthy rate but losing them just as fast, no amount of new pipeline will fix the revenue curve — the CRO's job is to see the whole net-revenue picture and prioritize the leak that matters most, which for many SaaS businesses is gross retention long before it is top-of-funnel volume. Owning expansion and renewal, not just new logos, is the clearest tell that you have hired a genuine revenue leader rather than a sales manager with a bigger title.

It is worth being concrete about how retention reframes priorities, because it is the least intuitive part of the role for a founder trained to equate growth with new logos. A business losing fifteen percent of its revenue to churn each year is running up a down escalator: every new dollar of bookings has to first replace a lost dollar before it counts as growth. Improving gross retention by even a few points can do more for the revenue curve than a comparable increase in new pipeline, and it is almost always cheaper to achieve, because keeping an existing customer costs a fraction of acquiring a new one. A fractional CRO who has seen enough companies knows to check the retention number early and, when it is the real problem, to have the discipline to fix the leak before pouring more water into the bucket.

## How much does a fractional CRO cost and what is the ROI
Pricing for fractional CROs varies by market, scope, and the operator's track record, but the common structures are a monthly retainer tied to a fixed number of days per month, sometimes paired with equity or a performance component linked to revenue milestones. The honest answer is that rates range widely and any specific number quoted as universal is marketing, not fact — a lightly-tenured operator in a small market and a former public-company CRO command very different fees. What you should evaluate is not the raw rate but the ratio of that cost to a comparable full-time package once you load in base salary, bonus, benefits, and equity for a full-time revenue chief.

The ROI case rests on three things. First, speed: a seasoned fractional CRO has run this diagnostic dozens of times and compresses into ninety days what an internal first-time leader might take a year to figure out. Second, cost avoidance: you get executive judgment without the full-time executive burn, and you avoid the far larger cost of a mis-hired full-time CRO, which for an early-stage company can set revenue back a year or more. Third, transferability: a good engagement is designed to make the CRO unnecessary — they build systems and coach the internal team so that when the engagement ends, the capability stays. The frameworks for evaluating that build-versus-buy decision are laid out at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-vs-full-time.

There is a fourth, less-discussed source of ROI: pattern recognition. A fractional CRO who has worked across a dozen companies carries a library of failure modes and their fixes that no first-time internal hire can match. They have seen the specific way a usage-based pricing model distorts comp incentives, the specific reason a PLG motion stalls when it tries to bolt on enterprise sales, the specific CRM misconfiguration that makes every forecast optimistic. That accumulated pattern library means they rarely have to learn on your dime; they recognize the shape of your problem from the first week and skip straight to the intervention that has worked elsewhere. Paying for that experience part-time is often the single most capital-efficient revenue investment an early-stage company can make.

When you actually run the comparison against a full-time hire, remember to count the hidden costs on the other side of the ledger. A full-time CRO carries not just salary and equity but recruiting fees, onboarding time, the opportunity cost of a months-long search, and the very real risk that the hire is wrong — a mis-hire at the executive level typically costs far more than the person's compensation once you add the wasted quarters, the team turnover in their wake, and the strategy whiplash of reversing their decisions. A fractional engagement is, among other things, a way to buy down that risk: you get to see how a senior operator thinks and works before anyone commits to a permanent, high-stakes relationship.

The failure mode to watch for is an engagement that never ends because the CRO made themselves load-bearing instead of building a self-sustaining system. Structure the engagement with an explicit outcome and a rough time horizon — for example, a trustworthy forecast and a repeatable motion within two quarters — so that "success" has a definition both sides agree on before the first invoice.

## When should a company hire a fractional CRO and when should it not
The clearest signal that it's time is a plateau: revenue has stalled and the founder or a first sales hire can no longer personally carry the number, but the company is not yet big or complex enough to justify a full-time CRO. Other strong signals include a forecast that is wrong every quarter, a sales team that closes inconsistently with no shared methodology, marketing and sales openly blaming each other, or a CRM so unreliable that leadership makes decisions on gut feel. Any one of these is a systems gap that a fractional CRO is built to close.

A common and specific version of this signal is the "founder-led sales ceiling." In the earliest stage, the founder *is* the revenue engine — they close deals through sheer product conviction and relationship, and it works because buyers want to talk to the person who built the thing. But that motion doesn't transfer. The moment the company hires its first two or three reps and discovers they can't reproduce the founder's results, it has hit the ceiling: the company has proven that *someone* can sell the product, but not that the product can be sold as a *system*. That gap — between founder magic and a repeatable motion anyone competent can run — is the single most common reason a fractional CRO gets hired, and it is exactly the gap the role is designed to close.

There are also clear cases where a fractional CRO is the wrong hire. If the company has genuinely not found product-market fit, no revenue system will save it — the problem is upstream of go-to-market, and a CRO will spend the engagement building machinery for a product the market doesn't yet want. If the founder is unwilling to give the CRO real authority over comp, hiring, and process, the engagement will stall, because the entire value of the role comes from the ability to change the seams between functions. And if what the company actually needs is more feet on the street executing a motion that already works, a fractional VP of Sales or additional reps is the cheaper, better fit. Matching the seniority of the hire to the actual nature of the gap is the single most important decision here, and it's explored further at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/when-to-hire-revenue-leader.

The product-market-fit caveat deserves an honest gut-check, because it is the most expensive mistake a founder can make here. It is tempting, when growth stalls, to conclude that the problem is execution — that with a better sales system the numbers would come. Sometimes that's true. But sometimes the stall is the market telling you the product isn't yet solving a problem people will reliably pay to fix, and a fractional CRO hired into that situation will spend two quarters building a beautiful, disciplined machine that has nothing real to sell. The honest test is whether the customers you already have are retaining and expanding, and whether the deals you close are closing because of genuine pull rather than heroic push. If the answer is no, the work is upstream, and no revenue leader — fractional or full-time — can substitute for a product the market actually wants. A good fractional CRO will tell you this in the first month rather than take your money to paper over it, and that willingness to diagnose the real problem is itself one of the clearest signs you've hired the right one.

## Related questions
### How is a fractional CRO different from a sales consultant?
A consultant delivers recommendations and leaves; a fractional CRO owns the revenue number, sits at the executive table, and stays to install and run the systems they design, coaching the team until the motion is self-sustaining.

### Can a fractional CRO also fix marketing and customer success?
Yes — the "revenue" in the title means they own the full arc from demand through retention and expansion, not just sales. Fixing the handoffs between those functions is often where the biggest gains hide.

### How long does a typical fractional CRO engagement last?
Most run six to eighteen months: roughly a quarter to diagnose and rebuild the broken systems, then several more to install the operating cadence and coach the internal team before a planned handoff.

### Does a fractional CRO replace the need for a full-time CRO later?
Often it bridges to one. As complexity grows, many companies transition from fractional to full-time — and a good fractional CRO helps define the role and even interview the permanent hire they'll hand off to.

### Will a fractional CRO carry a sales quota themselves?
Usually not directly. They own the team's aggregate number and forecast, but their job is to build the system and coach reps to hit quota, not to personally close deals — that would defeat the transferability that justifies the role.

## FAQ
**What does CRO stand for?**
Chief Revenue Officer — the executive accountable for all revenue-generating functions: sales, the marketing-to-sales handoff, revenue operations, and customer retention and expansion.

**How many hours a week does a fractional CRO work per client?**
Typically ten to twenty-five hours, or one to three days a week per client, deliberately concentrated on the activities that move the revenue number rather than spread across a full-time schedule.

**Can a startup afford a fractional CRO?**
Often yes — that's the point of the model. A fractional engagement gives a company doing single-digit-millions in ARR access to executive-level revenue leadership for a fraction of a full-time package it couldn't otherwise justify.

**What's the difference between a fractional CRO and a fractional VP of Sales?**
Scope. A fractional VP of Sales fixes the sales team's execution; a fractional CRO owns the entire revenue engine, including marketing alignment, RevOps, pricing, and retention — the seams between functions, not just the sellers.

**How do you measure whether a fractional CRO is working?**
By the same metrics as a full-time CRO: pipeline coverage and quality, forecast accuracy, win rate, sales cycle length, net revenue retention, and — most importantly — whether the systems keep running after they step back.

**What industries use fractional CROs most?**
B2B SaaS and technology firms are the heaviest users because their revenue motions are complex and systems-dependent, but the model works for any company with a repeatable sales process — professional services, manufacturing, and healthcare tech among them.

**Does a fractional CRO hire and fire reps?**
They typically own the recommendation and the process — defining roles, running the interview loop, and setting performance standards — while final hiring and firing decisions are made jointly with the founder or CEO, since the CRO is part-time.

**What happens when the engagement ends?**
A well-run engagement ends with a documented, self-sustaining revenue system, a trained internal team, and a trustworthy forecast — plus, often, a defined plan for whether and when to hire a full-time successor.

**Can one fractional CRO serve several companies at once?**
Yes, and most do — that's what makes the model economical. A disciplined operator typically caps themselves at two to four concurrent clients so each still gets genuine executive attention rather than a thinly-spread name on a retainer.

**How is success different from a full-time CRO's success?**
The metrics are the same, but the finish line is different: a full-time CRO's job is to keep running the engine, while a fractional CRO's job is explicitly to build an engine that no longer needs them, then leave it running.
